does-the-de-minimis-exemption-still-appl.text:
← Import landed cost calculator

Does the $800 de minimis exemption still apply?

Until 2025, a shipment valued at $800 or less could generally enter the US without paying duty at all — the "de minimis" exemption. That coverage has been narrowed or eliminated for a growing set of countries and shipment types since then, most visibly for goods originating in or shipped from China and Hong Kong, and the rules have changed more than once. If you built your pricing around shipping small parcels duty-free, that assumption is exactly the kind of thing worth re-checking before your next order lands.

Not a customs broker or compliance service. This page and this calculator are not a customs broker, freight forwarder, or licensed customs classification service. They do not determine your HTS code, your duty rate, or your compliance obligations, and coverage of the de minimis exemption varies by origin country and shipment type and continues to change — verify your own shipment's status with a licensed customs broker or current CBP guidance.

What it costs when the exemption no longer applies

A worked example: a $200 item, $20 freight to the US, no supplemental tariff, an informal entry, shipped by air (no Harbor Maintenance Fee). At a 3% duty rate on the $220 customs value:

Line itemAmount
Item cost$200.00
Freight$20.00
Duty (3% of $220 customs value)$6.60
Merchandise Processing Fee (informal, flat)$2.62
Customs broker fee$5.00
Total landed cost$234.22

That is $14.22 of duty and fees on a shipment that would have landed at exactly $220 under the old duty-free exemption — a 4.61% tariff burden on the $200 item cost that a seller pricing off the old assumption would not have budgeted for. On a shipment with a nonzero Section 301 or supplemental rate, or a higher duty rate, that gap is larger. Run your own numbers on the calculator, pre-filled with this example.

Common questions

Does the $800 de minimis exemption still apply to my shipment?

For a growing set of countries and shipment types, no — the exemption that let shipments valued under $800 enter the US duty-free has been narrowed or eliminated since 2025, most visibly for goods originating in or shipped from China and Hong Kong. Coverage has changed more than once and varies by origin country and shipment type, so check current CBP guidance or ask your customs broker for your specific lane rather than assuming either the old or the new rule applies by default.

What changes for a small seller who used to ship duty-free under $800?

A shipment that used to clear with zero duty, zero tariff, and no processing fee now goes through the same arithmetic as a larger, always-dutiable shipment: duty on the customs value, any applicable supplemental or Section 301 tariff, and a Merchandise Processing Fee (flat for an informal entry, percentage-based with a floor and ceiling for a formal one). On the worked example above — a $200 item, $20 freight, no supplemental tariff, informal entry, air freight — that is $14.22 of fees that used to be $0.

How do I find out for sure whether my shipment is covered?

This page and this calculator are not a customs classification or compliance determination — they price the arithmetic once you know your rates. Confirm your shipment's actual de minimis status, HTS classification, and duty rate with a licensed customs broker or directly against current CBP guidance before you rely on either the old or the new assumption in your pricing.

formal-vs-informal-entry.html.text:
← Import landed cost calculator

Formal or informal entry — why the fee jumps $30 either way you guess

The Merchandise Processing Fee is priced two completely different ways depending on one checkbox: a flat $2.62 for an informal entry, or 0.3464% of customs value — with a $32.71 floor and a $634.62 ceiling — for a formal one. Guess wrong on a mid-size shipment and the fee you priced is off by $30, not by a rounding error.

Not a customs broker or compliance service. This page and the calculator it links to are not a customs broker, freight forwarder, or licensed customs classification service. Whether a specific shipment qualifies for informal entry depends on commodity type and your broker's own practice, not only on value — confirm which applies to you with a licensed customs broker or current CBP guidance before you rely on either entry type in your pricing.

The line is usually $2,500 of customs value

Customs value — item cost plus freight to the US port or border, the same basis this calculator uses — at or under $2,500 is generally eligible for informal entry. Above that, a formal entry is generally required. A few commodity types (certain textiles among them) carry a lower threshold, and a broker can sometimes elect formal entry below $2,500 for their own consolidated tracking, so treat $2,500 as the general rule rather than a determination for your specific goods.

What the floor actually does to the fee

0.3464% of customs value is a small number until the value is large. Solved against the $32.71 floor, the percentage only clears it above about $9,443 of customs value — so every formal entry below that figure pays the same flat $32.71 the floor sets, not a value-scaled fee. The percentage does not start doing anything until a shipment is nearly four times the informal-entry threshold.

Customs valueInformal MPFFormal MPFFormal − informal
$2,500$2.62$32.71 (floor)$30.09
$9,000$2.62$32.71 (floor)$30.09
$20,000$2.62$69.28 (0.3464%)$66.66

At $2,500 and at $9,000 the formal-entry fee is identical — $32.71 — because both sit under the ~$9,443 crossover where the floor is still the binding number. Only at $20,000, well past that crossover, does the percentage actually exceed the floor and the fee starts scaling with value. Run either row on the calculator, pre-filled at $2,500 customs value and flip the entry type to see the $30.09 move by itself, with every other input held still.

MPF figures are the published CBP fee schedule as of this tool's last update and are indexed periodically — confirm current figures at cbp.gov before relying on them for a real entry.

Common questions

What decides whether my shipment is a formal or an informal entry?

Customs value is the usual line: shipments valued at $2,500 or less are generally eligible for informal entry, and shipments above that generally require a formal entry. Some commodity types (certain textiles, for example) have a lower threshold, and a broker can sometimes elect a formal entry below $2,500 for their own tracking reasons — so this is the general rule, not a determination for your specific shipment. Confirm which applies with your customs broker or current CBP guidance.

Why does the Merchandise Processing Fee jump by $30 right at the line?

Informal entries pay a flat $2.62 regardless of value. Formal entries pay 0.3464% of customs value, but with a statutory floor of $32.71 per entry — and that floor is higher than the percentage would produce for any formal entry under roughly $9,443 of customs value. So a $2,500 formal entry does not pay a $2,500-sized fee; it pays the same $32.71 floor a $9,000 formal entry pays. The jump from informal to formal is $30.09, flat, no matter which side of $2,500 the shipment sits on, right up to that ceiling.

Does the $32.71 floor change with the size of my shipment?

Not below about $9,443 of customs value — 0.3464% of any formal-entry shipment under that figure comes out below $32.71, so the floor is what actually gets charged. Above roughly $9,443 the percentage takes over and the fee scales with value up to the $634.62 statutory ceiling, reached around $183,200 of customs value.

Is my shipment data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator this page links to runs entirely in your browser. Nothing you type is sent to a server, there is no account, and the optional usage counter only tallies anonymous feature events, never your costs, rates, or quantities.

index.html.text:
FOR SMALL IMPORTERS & E-COMMERCE SELLERS

What does this shipment actually cost, landed?

Enter your item cost, freight, and the duty and supplemental tariff rates from your own HTS lookup or broker to see total landed cost, cost per unit, and the tariff burden as a percent of your invoice price — the number that turns a profitable-looking import into a loss when it shows up at customs instead of at pricing time. See whether the $800 de minimis exemption still applies to your shipment before you assume the old duty-free math still holds, and why the processing fee jumps $30 the moment an entry is formal instead of informal, regardless of how close the shipment sits to the value line. Compare this against tracking landed cost by hand on this calculator vs. a spreadsheet, or against booking through a freight forwarder on this calculator vs. Flexport.

Not a customs broker or compliance service. This tool is not a customs broker, freight forwarder, or licensed customs classification service. It does not determine your HTS code, your duty rate, or your compliance obligations — you must verify those with a licensed customs broker or CBP. This tool only performs the arithmetic once you supply the rates and fees.

MPF and HMF percentages, floors and ceilings are the currently published CBP fee schedule figures as of this tool's last update — confirm current figures at cbp.gov before relying on them.

Common questions

Does this tool know my product's actual duty rate?

No, on purpose. The duty rate and the supplemental/Section 301 tariff rate are fields you fill in, not a stored schedule this tool claims to know. Duty rates are set per HTS classification and change; a table baked into a calculator goes stale silently and still looks authoritative. Look your product's HTS code up at hts.usitc.gov, or confirm the current rate with a licensed customs broker, then type it in — the arithmetic is yours to check.

Is this a customs broker or a compliance service?

No. This is not a customs broker, freight forwarder, or licensed customs classification service. It does not determine your HTS code, your duty rate, or your compliance obligations — you must verify those with a licensed customs broker or CBP. This tool only performs the arithmetic once you supply the rates and fees.

What is the Merchandise Processing Fee?

A CBP fee charged on most formal entries: 0.3464% of the customs value, with a minimum of $32.71 and a maximum of $634.62 per entry. Informal entries (typically lower-value, more casual shipments) pay a flat fee instead, currently around $2.62. These are published, indexed figures — confirm the current numbers at cbp.gov before relying on them for a real entry, since CBP periodically adjusts them. See formal vs. informal entry for what decides which one you are and why the fee does not scale smoothly across that line.

What is the Harbor Maintenance Fee, and why does it only sometimes apply?

It is 0.125% of the customs value, charged on shipments that move by ocean freight — not on air or truck shipments. Check the ocean freight box if your shipment came by sea; leave it unchecked otherwise. Like the MPF, this is a published CBP fee schedule figure worth confirming before relying on it.

What does the 2025 end of the $800 de minimis exemption mean for me?

For many countries, shipments that used to clear duty-free under $800 no longer do, so imports that once had no landed-cost surprise at all now carry duty, potential supplemental tariffs, and processing fees the way a formal or informal entry always has. If you used to ship under that exemption, run your numbers through this calculator rather than assuming the old duty-free math still holds — see does the de minimis exemption still apply for the specifics and how to check where things stand for your own shipments.

Is my shipment data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. The shareable link carries your numbers in the URL itself rather than sending them to a server. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your costs, rates, or quantities.

vs-flexport.html.text:
← Import landed cost calculator

This calculator vs. Flexport

Two different shapes: Flexport is a freight forwarder and customs brokerage you sign up for as an ongoing account — it books the shipment, moves the freight, and files the customs entry. This page is a free, private worksheet for one narrower question: given the item cost, freight quote, and duty or supplemental tariff rate you already have, what does this shipment land at, per unit, and what share of the invoice price is tariff.

Flexport's own pricing and account terms are not reachable from this session to confirm today's figures, so no dollar amount for Flexport appears anywhere on this page — only its well-documented identity and category (a freight forwarder and customs brokerage sold as an ongoing account relationship) are stated.

This calculator does not book freight, does not file a customs entry, and stores nothing on a server. It takes an item cost, freight cost, duty rate, Section 301/supplemental tariff rate, an ocean-freight toggle for the Harbor Maintenance Fee, and a formal/informal-entry toggle for the Merchandise Processing Fee, and turns that into total landed cost, cost per unit, and tariff burden as a percent of invoice price. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need a forwarder to book this shipment, move the freight, and file the customs entry.Flexport, or a comparable freight forwarder — that is not something this calculator does.
Given the item cost, freight quote, and duty rate I already have, what does this shipment land at per unit?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
Did I apply the MPF floor/ceiling and the ocean-only HMF condition correctly?This calculator applies both automatically on every calculation.
Does the de minimis exemption still apply to this shipment?This calculator's de minimis check.
What is my actual HTS classification and duty rate?Flexport, a licensed customs broker, or your own HTS lookup — this calculator prices a rate you already have, it does not classify goods.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. Flexport is used through an ongoing account relationship.

What this page is not

This calculator is not a replacement for Flexport, or for a freight forwarder or customs broker generally. It does not book freight, does not file a customs entry, and does not determine an HTS classification or a duty rate. Most importers who ship through a forwarder get different value from each: Flexport (or a comparable forwarder) for booking, moving, and filing the shipment as an ongoing service, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login check of what a shipment lands at per unit before you commit to it.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Flexport?

They do different jobs and a small importer who ships through a forwarder will likely use both. Flexport is a freight forwarder and customs brokerage: it books the shipment, moves the freight, files the customs entry, and is sold as an ongoing account relationship with its own onboarding, rather than a self-service arithmetic tool. This calculator does one narrower thing, before or alongside that: starting from an item cost, a freight quote, and a duty or supplemental tariff rate you already have from your own HTS lookup or broker, it works out total landed cost, cost per unit, and the tariff burden as a percent of the invoice price, applying the Merchandise Processing Fee's floor and ceiling and the Harbor Maintenance Fee's ocean-only condition automatically. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and does not book or move anything. An importer who wants a forwarder to handle booking, customs filing, and compliance end to end is better served by Flexport or a comparable freight forwarder; someone who already has a quote and a duty rate and wants an instant, private answer to what a shipment lands at per unit is in the right place here.

Does Flexport already show me landed cost?

Flexport's own platform is built around managing shipments booked through it, with visibility into the freight and duty it is handling for your account. This calculator is not a replacement for that: it is a quick, private worksheet for pricing a shipment before you book it, or for checking a quote or a self-filed entry's arithmetic against the Merchandise Processing Fee and Harbor Maintenance Fee rules by hand, with no account and nothing sent anywhere.

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Flexport, Inc. Flexport is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.

vs-tracking-landed-cost-in-a-spreadsheet.text:
← Import landed cost calculator

This calculator vs. tracking landed cost in a spreadsheet

Names no specific product or company — this compares a free calculator against the generic method most importers already use: a personal or shared spreadsheet with a formula for duty and fees typed in once and copied down.

QuestionSpreadsheet formulaThis calculator
Merchandise Processing Fee floor/ceilingUsually a flat percentage typed once — the $32.71 floor and $634.62 ceiling on formal entries are easy to forget and silently wrong at the edgesApplies the floor and ceiling on every calculation, on the current published CBP figures
Harbor Maintenance FeeEither always applied or always omitted, depending on what the sheet's original author shippedToggled by an explicit ocean-freight checkbox, applied only when checked
Formal vs. informal entryUsually one formula per sheet, not switched per shipmentA single toggle switches the whole MPF calculation between the two schedules
Per-unit cost and tariff burden %An extra column you have to remember to add and keep in sync with the totalComputed automatically alongside the total
History across shipmentsIts actual strength — a running log with supplier, tracking number, and margin per shipmentPrices one shipment at a time; does not replace a shipment log
Shareable single scenarioRequires sending the whole file or a screenshotOne link, via "Copy shareable link," with no file attached

Neither tool determines your HTS classification, your actual duty rate, or your compliance obligations — both are arithmetic on numbers you already have, and both are only as accurate as the rates you type in.

Common questions

Why not just track landed cost in a spreadsheet?

Plenty of importers do, and a spreadsheet is a fine tool for tracking a history of shipments over time. The failure mode is not the spreadsheet itself — it is the Merchandise Processing Fee's floor and ceiling and the Harbor Maintenance Fee's ocean-only condition, both of which are easy to type once and forget to update when a shipment's value crosses the floor, the ceiling, or the ocean-vs-air line. A calculator that recomputes those conditions on every input avoids that particular drift; a spreadsheet formula copied down a column does not check itself.

Does this calculator replace my spreadsheet?

Not necessarily. This tool prices one shipment at a time and does not save a history across sessions the way a spreadsheet's rows do. Many importers use both: this calculator to get one shipment's arithmetic right, including the MPF/HMF edge cases, and their own spreadsheet to log the result alongside supplier, tracking number, and margin for every shipment over a season.
